title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Time Series Databases
summary: A time series database (TSDB) is a database optimized for storing and querying timestamped data points — sequences of (timestamp, value) pairs tagged with metadata (metric name, labels) — where writes are append-only and…
objectives: Why are time series databases 10–100× faster than general-purpose databases for time-series workloads?
Explain delta-of-delta timestamp encoding and Gorilla float encoding.
What is downsampling, and why is it critical for time series at scale?
Compare InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Prometheus, and QuestDB. When do you choose each?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A **time series database (TSDB)** is a database optimized for storing and querying *timestamped data points* — sequences of `(timestamp, value)` pairs tagged with metadata (metric name, labels) — where writes are append-only and high-volume, reads are time-range scans with aggregations (avg, max, p99), and the storage engine exploits time locality (columnar compression, delta-encoding, downsampling) to deliver 10–100× the throughput of a general-purpose DB on time-ordered workloads, exemplified by **InfluxDB**, **TimescaleDB**, **Prometheus**, **QuestDB**, and **Amazon Timestream**, and used for **infrastructure metrics, application APM, IoT sensor data, financial market data, and observability stacks**.

Time series data has a distinctive shape: each data point is a `(timestamp, metric_name, labels, value)` tuple, where labels are key-value pairs (`{host=web-1, region=us-east, env=prod}`) that identify the source. The data is *write-heavy* (millions of points per second from thousands of sources), *append-only* (you never update old points), *time-ordered* (queries are almost always time-range scans), and *aggregation-heavy* (raw points are rarely queried; users want `avg(cpu_usage) over 5m windows grouped by host`). General-purpose databases struggle because their storage engines optimize for random access and updates — exactly what time series doesn't need. A time series database exploits the workload's structure: writes are sequential appends (LSM-trees or columnar append-only files), timestamps are delta-encoded (consecutive points differ by a fixed interval, so storing deltas compresses 10×), floats are Gorilla-encoded (XOR-based compression exploiting small inter-sample changes), and strings (metric names, label values) are dictionary-encoded. The result: InfluxDB can ingest millions of points per second per node, vs. ~10k inserts/sec for a generic PostgreSQL on the same hardware.

The **data model** varies across TSDBs. **InfluxDB** (the most popular purpose-built TSDB, Go-based, OpenTSDB successor) uses *measurements, tags, and fields*: a measurement is `cpu_usage`, tags are indexed dimensions (`host=web-1, region=us-east`), fields are the actual values (`value=0.42`). Tags are indexed; fields are not. Queries use InfluxQL (SQL-like) or Flux (functional pipeline). **Prometheus** (CNCF, the de facto standard for Kubernetes monitoring) uses *metric name + labels*: `cpu_usage{host="web-1",region="us-east"}`. All labels are indexed. Queries use PromQL, a functional query language optimized for time-series operations (`rate(http_requests_total[5m])`, `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))`). **TimescaleDB** is a PostgreSQL extension that adds *hypertables* — automatic partitioning by time (each chunk is a regular PostgreSQL table), with all PostgreSQL features (JOINs, JSON, GIS, transactions) intact. This makes it ideal for teams already on PostgreSQL. **QuestDB** is a column-oriented TSDB with SQL syntax and very high ingest throughput (claims millions of rows/sec). **Amazon Timestream** is the managed AWS option, with time-based tiering (memory -> SSD -> S3) and a SQL query interface. **Druid** is technically a real-time analytics database but is widely used for time-series workloads (Wikipedia uses it for edit analytics; Netflix for viewing metrics).

The **storage engine** innovations are what make TSDBs fast. **(1) Columnar layout** — within a time chunk, timestamps, tag values, and fields are stored in separate columns, enabling efficient scans of a single metric over many time points without reading unrelated data. **(2) Delta-of-delta timestamp encoding** — for regularly-sampled data (every 10s), consecutive timestamps differ by 10, and the differences-of-differences are 0, encoding to ~1 bit per timestamp (vs. 64 bits uncompressed). **(3) Gorilla float encoding** — floats are XOR'd with the previous value; if the XOR has few significant bits, only those are stored. Real-world metrics (CPU, memory, latency) change slowly, so 10× compression is typical. **(4) Dictionary encoding** — tag values (`host=web-1`) are stored once in a dictionary and referenced by integer ID. **(5) Time-based partitioning (chunking)** — data is sharded into time chunks (1h, 1d); queries touching only recent data scan only recent chunks; old chunks can be downsampled or moved to cheaper storage. **(6) Downsampling (rollups)** — pre-compute aggregates (avg, max, p99) over windows (1m, 5m, 1h, 1d) and store them alongside raw data; queries for `avg(cpu) over 1h window` read the pre-computed rollup instead of scanning raw points. **(7) Retention policies** — automatically expire or downsample old data (e.g., raw for 7 days, 5m rollups for 30 days, 1h rollups for 1 year). These techniques collectively deliver 10–100× compression and 10× query speedup vs. general-purpose DBs.

Real-world deployments illustrate the scale. **Netflix's metrics pipeline** ingests billions of data points per day from thousands of microservices — CPU, memory, request latency, error rates, custom business metrics. They use Atlas (an in-house TSDB, open-sourced) for high-resolution metrics and Elasticsearch for log analytics. The pipeline supports real-time dashboards (Grafana), autoscaling decisions (if CPU > 70% for 5m, scale up), and alerting (if error rate > 1% for 2m, page on-call). **Uber's observability stack** (M3) processes millions of metrics per second across tens of thousands of hosts — they open-sourced M3 as a Prometheus-compatible TSDB at Uber scale. Uber uses M3 for infrastructure monitoring, business metrics (trips per minute per city), and SLI/SLO tracking. **Pinterest uses OpenTSDB** (HBase-backed) for similar metrics. **Cloudflare** uses ClickHouse (column-oriented) for their analytics, with billions of rows per day. **Discord uses Cassandra** for time-series message storage, taking advantage of wide-column time-ordered clustering. **The New York Times uses TimescaleDB** for tracking article engagement metrics. **Tesla uses InfluxDB** for vehicle telemetry (battery, motor, location per second per vehicle — millions of vehicles). The pattern: any workload producing timestamped measurements at scale is a TSDB candidate.

The trade-offs explain why TSDBs are specialized tools rather than defaults. First, **limited query patterns** — TSDBs optimize for time-range scans with aggregations; arbitrary joins, ACID transactions, or ad-hoc queries are weak. TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL extension) is the exception — it inherits PostgreSQL's full query power. Second, **schema rigidity** — most TSDBs expect a fixed schema per measurement (you declare the tags and fields up front); schema evolution is awkward. Third, **cardinality limits** — Prometheus and InfluxDB struggle with high-cardinality labels (e.g., `user_id` as a label = millions of series); each series has overhead. Mitigations: don't use high-cardinality values as labels (use logs for that), or use TSDBs designed for high cardinality (TimescaleDB, Druid, ClickHouse). Fourth, **operational complexity** — TSDBs at scale need capacity planning (storage grows linearly with retention), compaction tuning, retention policy management, and downsampling pipeline maintenance. Fifth, **no updates** — TSDBs are append-only; correcting bad data is awkward (you'd write a compensating point or wait for retention to drop it). Sixth, **real-time vs. historical trade-off** — high-resolution recent data (1s intervals) is expensive to retain; downsampling policies trade resolution for storage. Seventh, **ecosystem fit** — Prometheus has the richest Kubernetes/observability ecosystem (Grafana, Alertmanager, service discovery); InfluxDB has Telegraf (collection agent) and Kapacitor (alerting); TimescaleDB fits PostgreSQL teams. The takeaway: TSDBs are the right tool when the workload is timestamped, write-heavy, aggregation-focused, and time-range-scanned — and they dominate the observability and IoT spaces precisely because these workloads fit the model.

WHERE time > now()-1h
GROUP BY host, time(5m)"] end CHUNK --> Q ROLL --> Q subgraph Consumers["Consumers"] GRAF["Grafana dashboards"] ALERT["Alertmanager
(page on-call if error > 1%)"] AUTO["Autoscaler
(scale if CPU > 70%)"] ML["Anomaly detection"] end Q --> GRAF Q --> ALERT Q --> AUTO Q --> ML ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Time series data point shape: (timestamp, metric_name, labels, value) 1.7B cpu_usage {host=web-1, region=us-east} 0.42 Storage engine optimizations (why TSDBs are 10-100x faster): +---------------------+-------------------------+--------------------+ | Optimization | What it does | Compression | +---------------------+-------------------------+--------------------+ | Columnar layout | ts, tags, fields stored | scan one metric | | | in separate columns | without reading | | | | unrelated data | | Delta-of-delta ts | store diff-of-diff of | ~1 bit/ts (vs 64) | | | consecutive timestamps | (regular sampling) | | Gorilla float XOR | XOR float with previous | 10x for slow- | | | value; store sig bits | changing metrics | | Dictionary strings | tag values -> int ID | deduplication | | Time-based chunking | partition by 1h/1d | scan only relevant | | | | chunks | | Downsampling rollups| precompute avg/max/p99 | query rollup not | | | over 1m/5m/1h windows | raw points | | Retention policies | auto-expire or downsample| bound storage | +---------------------+-------------------------+--------------------+ Write path (append-only, LSM-tree): point -> batch -> memtable (RAM) -> flush SSTable (sequential disk) -> compaction merges + downsamples old chunks Read path (time-range scan): query -> identify chunks in range -> bloom filter -> read columns -> aggregate (avg/max/p99 over window) -> return Real-world scale: Netflix Atlas: billions of points/day Uber M3: millions of points/sec Tesla InfluxDB: millions of vehicles x telemetry/sec Cloudflare ClickHouse: billions of rows/day ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A metric collector (Telegraf agent, Prometheus scraper, or application directly) batches data points and writes to the TSDB. The TSDB ingester appends to an LSM-tree MemTable (in-memory) — O(1) sequential write, ~1M points/sec per node. Periodically, the MemTable flushes to disk as an immutable SSTable, sorted by `(metric, labels, timestamp)`. Compression is applied: timestamps are delta-of-delta encoded (regular sampling → ~1 bit per ts), floats are Gorilla-XOR encoded (slow-changing values → 10× compression), strings are dictionary-encoded. 2. Background compaction merges SSTables and applies downsampling: every 1m, compute `avg`, `max`, `p99` of raw points and store as a rollup. Old raw data is expired per retention policy (e.g., raw 7 days, 5m rollups 30 days, 1h rollups 1 year). Time-based chunking ensures queries touching recent data scan only recent chunks; queries touching historical data use the appropriate rollup resolution. 3. A query like `SELECT avg(value) FROM cpu WHERE time > now()-1h AND host='web-1' GROUP BY time(5m)` is executed by: identifying the time chunks in the last hour, reading the `cpu` metric's value column (columnar scan), filtering by `host='web-1'` (using the label index), bucketing points into 5m windows, computing the average per bucket, and returning the result. If a 5m rollup exists, the query uses it directly (no raw scan). Real-world: Netflix's Atlas returns such queries in <100ms over billions of points, powering real-time Grafana dashboards used by every engineering team.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Time series store mock: append-only points, columnar storage simulation, downsampling (rollups), and time-range aggregation queries.
- Append-only time series store with chunking + downsampling.
- points = list of (metric, labels, value, ts).
- Pre-compute avg/max for each time window.
- Series_key -> list of (ts, value) sorted by ts
- Series_key = (metric, frozenset(labels.items()))
- Downsampled rollups: series_key -> {window_s: [(bucket_ts, count, sum, max)]}
- Use rollup if we have one for this window

**Defines:** `TimeSeriesStore`, `delta_of_delta_encode()`, `gorilla_xor_encode()`

```python
"""
Time series store mock: append-only points, columnar storage simulation,
downsampling (rollups), and time-range aggregation queries.

Demonstrates:
  - Append-only ingestion (LSM-style MemTable)
  - Delta-of-delta timestamp encoding (compression)
  - Gorilla-style float XOR encoding (compression)
  - Time-based chunking (1-minute partitions)
  - Downsampling: pre-compute avg/max for 1m, 5m windows
  - Time-range queries with GROUP BY time(window)

Models a simplified InfluxDB/TimescaleDB-style single-node TSDB.

Run:  python3 tsdb.py
"""

import time
import math
import struct
from collections import defaultdict

class TimeSeriesStore:
    """Append-only time series store with chunking + downsampling."""

    def __init__(self):
        # series_key -> list of (ts, value) sorted by ts
        # series_key = (metric, frozenset(labels.items()))
        self._series = defaultdict(list)
        # downsampled rollups: series_key -> {window_s: [(bucket_ts, count, sum, max)]}
        self._rollups = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(list))
        self._raw_retention_seconds = 3600  # keep raw points for 1h
        self._stats = {"points_ingested": 0, "rollups_computed": 0,
                       "points_expired": 0}

    # ----- ingestion -----
    def write(self, metric, labels, value, ts=None):
        ts = ts or time.time()
        key = (metric, frozenset(labels.items()))
        self._series[key].append((ts, value))
        self._stats["points_ingested"] += 1

    def write_batch(self, points):
        """points = list of (metric, labels, value, ts)."""
        for metric, labels, value, ts in points:
            self.write(metric, labels, value, ts)

    # ----- downsampling (rollups) -----
    def downsample(self, metric, labels, window_seconds):
        """Pre-compute avg/max for each time window."""
        key = (metric, frozenset(labels.items()))
        points = self._series[key]
        if not points:
            return
        buckets = defaultdict(list)
        for ts, val in points:
            bucket_ts = math.floor(ts / window_seconds) * window_seconds
            buckets[bucket_ts].append(val)
        rollup = [(bts, len(vals), sum(vals), max(vals))
                  for bts, vals in sorted(buckets.items())]
        self._rollups[key][window_seconds] = rollup
        self._stats["rollups_computed"] += len(rollup)

    # ----- query -----
    def query(self, metric, labels, start_ts, end_ts, aggregator="avg",
              window_seconds=None):
        """Time-range query with optional GROUP BY time(window).

        Uses downsampled rollup if available for the window.
        """
        key = (metric, frozenset(labels.items()))
        # Use rollup if we have one for this window
        if window_seconds and window_seconds in self._rollups.get(key, {}):
            results = []
            for bts, count, total, mx in self._rollups[key][window_seconds]:
                if start_ts <= bts < end_ts:
                    if aggregator == "avg":
                        results.append((bts, total / count if count else 0))
                    elif aggregator == "max":
                        results.append((bts, mx))
                    elif aggregator == "sum":
                        results.append((bts, total))
            return results
        # Otherwise scan raw points (slower)
        points = [(ts, val) for ts, val in self._series[key]
                  if start_ts <= ts < end_ts]
        if not window_seconds:
            if aggregator == "avg":
                return [(min(t for t, _ in points),
                         sum(v for _, v in points) / len(points))] if points else []
            elif aggregator == "max":
                return [(min(t for t, _ in points),
                         max(v for _, v in points))] if points else []
        # Group by window
        buckets = defaultdict(list)
        for ts, val in points:
            bucket_ts = math.floor(ts / window_seconds) * window_seconds
            buckets[bucket_ts].append(val)
        results = []
        for bts, vals in sorted(buckets.items()):
            if aggregator == "avg":
                results.append((bts, sum(vals) / len(vals)))
            elif aggregator == "max":
                results.append((bts, max(vals)))
            elif aggregator == "sum":
                results.append((bts, sum(vals)))
        return results

    # ----- retention -----
    def expire_old_points(self, now_ts=None):
        """Drop raw points older than retention window."""
        now_ts = now_ts or time.time()
        cutoff = now_ts - self._raw_retention_seconds
        for key in list(self._series.keys()):
            before = len(self._series[key])
            self._series[key] = [(ts, v) for ts, v in self._series[key] if ts >= cutoff]
            self._stats["points_expired"] += before - len(self._series[key])

    def stats(self):
        return dict(self._stats)

# ----- compression demonstration (delta-of-delta + Gorilla XOR) -----
def delta_of_delta_encode(timestamps):
    """Encode regular-sampled timestamps as delta-of-deltas.
    For regular sampling (every T sec), delta-of-deltas are 0 -> ~1 bit each."""
    if len(timestamps) < 3:
        return timestamps
    deltas = [timestamps[i+1] - timestamps[i] for i in range(len(timestamps)-1)]
    dod = [deltas[i+1] - deltas[i] for i in range(len(deltas)-1)]
    return dod  # if regular sampling, mostly zeros

def gorilla_xor_encode(values):
    """XOR consecutive floats; store only significant bits.
    Real-world metrics change slowly -> 10x compression typical."""
    if len(values) < 2:
        return values
    encoded = []
    prev_bits = struct.unpack(">Q", struct.pack(">d", values[0]))[0]
    for v in values[1:]:
        cur_bits = struct.unpack(">Q", struct.pack(">d", v))[0]
        xor = prev_bits ^ cur_bits
        # Real Gorilla: if xor == 0, store 1 bit (no change)
        #               if leading/trailing zeros match prev, store type+meaningful bits
        encoded.append(xor)
        prev_bits = cur_bits
    nonzero = sum(1 for x in encoded if x != 0)
    return {"total": len(encoded), "nonzero": nonzero,
            "compressed_bits_estimate": nonzero * 16 + (len(encoded) - nonzero) * 1}

# ---------------- demo ----------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    store = TimeSeriesStore()

    print("=== Ingest CPU metrics for host=web-1 (60s, 1 point/sec) ===")
    base_ts = 1_700_000_000
    for i in range(60):
        # Simulate slow-changing CPU usage (0.40-0.45 range)
        val = 0.40 + 0.02 * math.sin(i / 10) + 0.005 * (i % 3)
        store.write("cpu_usage", {"host": "web-1", "region": "us-east"},
                    val, ts=base_ts + i)

    print(f"  ingested: {store.stats()['points_ingested']} points")

    print("\n=== Compression demo (delta-of-delta + Gorilla XOR) ===")
    timestamps = [base_ts + i for i in range(60)]
    dod = delta_of_delta_encode(timestamps)
    print(f"  delta-of-deltas: {len(dod)} values, "
          f"{sum(1 for x in dod if x == 0)}/{len(dod)} are zero (regular sampling)")
    values = [0.40 + 0.02 * math.sin(i / 10) for i in range(60)]
    enc = gorilla_xor_encode(values)
    print(f"  Gorilla XOR: {enc['total']} values, "
          f"{enc['nonzero']} non-zero -> ~{enc['compressed_bits_estimate']} bits "
          f"(vs {enc['total']*64} uncompressed = "
          f"{(enc['total']*64) / enc['compressed_bits_estimate']:.1f}x compression)")

    print("\n=== Downsample to 5-second windows ===")
    store.downsample("cpu_usage", {"host": "web-1", "region": "us-east"}, 5)
    print(f"  rollups computed: {store.stats()['rollups_computed']}")

    print("\n=== Query: avg cpu_usage over last 60s, GROUP BY 5s (uses rollup) ===")
    results = store.query("cpu_usage", {"host": "web-1", "region": "us-east"},
                          base_ts, base_ts + 60, aggregator="avg", window_seconds=5)
    for bts, avg in results[:6]:
        print(f"  ts={bts}  avg={avg:.4f}")

    print("\n=== Query: max cpu_usage over last 60s (no window) ===")
    result = store.query("cpu_usage", {"host": "web-1", "region": "us-east"},
                         base_ts, base_ts + 60, aggregator="max")
    if result:
        print(f"  max={result[0][1]:.4f}")

    print("\n=== Expire raw points older than 1h retention ===")
    future_ts = base_ts + 4000  # 4000s later -> raw points are old
    store.expire_old_points(now_ts=future_ts)
    print(f"  points expired: {store.stats()['points_expired']}")
    print(f"  (downsampled rollups retained for historical queries)")

    print("\n=== Query after expiry (rollups still answer) ===")
    results = store.query("cpu_usage", {"host": "web-1", "region": "us-east"},
                          base_ts, base_ts + 60, aggregator="avg", window_seconds=5)
    print(f"  rollup-based query returned {len(results)} buckets (raw points expired)")

    print("\n  TSDB trade-offs:")
    print("    + 10-100x compression (delta-of-delta, Gorilla XOR, dictionary)")
    print("    + append-only writes -> millions of points/sec per node")
    print("    + downsampling rollups -> fast historical queries")
    print("    + retention policies -> bound storage growth")
    print("    - limited query patterns (time-range scans + aggregations)")
    print("    - high-cardinality labels cause series explosion")
    print("    - no updates (append-only); correcting bad data is awkward")
    print("    - operational complexity (retention, compaction, rollups)")
```

retention policy** specifies how long data is kept at each resolution.

Choose when: pure time-series workload, want turnkey TSDB with rich ecosystem, don't need SQL or joins.

quiz.question: Why do TSDBs struggle with high-cardinality labels, and how do you mitigate it?
options: Downsampling (also called rollups or aggregation) is the pre-computation of aggregates (avg, max, min, sum, p99, count) over fixed time windows (1m, 5m, 1h, 1d) from raw data points.
Uber built M3 (open-sourced, Prometheus-compatible) to handle scale that vanilla Prometheus couldn't.
Three structural advantages compound. (1) Storage engine matches the workload: TSDBs use LSM-trees or append-only columnar files because writes are append-only (never update old points).

quiz.explanation: High-cardinality labels (e.g., user_id, request_id, session_id as a label) cause series explosion. In Prometheus/InfluxDB, each unique combination of metric name + label values = one time series. If you have http_requests_total{user_id="..."} with 1M users, you have 1M series — each with its own in-memory index entry, chunk metadata, and ingestion path.
